papers.title: Astrocytes mobilize a broader repertoire of lysosomal repair mechanisms than neurons.
papers.summary: This paper compares how astrocytes and neurons respond to lysosomal membrane damage, a stress that can trigger cell dysfunction if not repaired. It finds that astrocytes have access to a wider range of lysosomal repair pathways compared to neurons, suggesting these two brain cell types differ substantially in their capacity to maintain lysosomal integrity. This implies neurons may be more vulnerable to lysosomal stress, which could have implications for neurodegeneration.
papers.why: Since lysosomal function is tightly linked to autophagy and mitophagy, understanding cell-type-specific differences in lysosomal repair capacity between astrocytes and neurons could help explain why neurons, including interneurons, are particularly susceptible to autophagic/mitophagic dysfunction in the brain.

papers.title: Fungal-Derived Decahydrofluorene Alkaloids Promote Mitochondrial Resilience and Neuroprotection in Cellular and Animal Models of Parkinson's Disease.
papers.summary: This paper describes newly identified fungal-derived compounds called decahydrofluorene alkaloids that appear to protect mitochondria from damage. The researchers tested these compounds in both cell-based and animal models of Parkinson's disease, a condition linked to mitochondrial dysfunction and neuronal loss. Their findings suggest these alkaloids help maintain mitochondrial health and protect neurons from degeneration.
papers.why: Since mitochondrial dysfunction and mitophagy are central to neurodegenerative processes in Parkinson's disease, this compound's neuroprotective mechanism could offer insights relevant to mitophagy pathways being studied in neurons, even though the paper's focus on peripheral dopaminergic neurons differs from the project's emphasis on interneurons and perineuronal nets.

papers.title: Association between p-tau181 in cerebrospinal fluid and shunt response in patients with normal-pressure hydrocephalus.
papers.summary: This study examines whether levels of p-tau181, a tau protein biomarker, in cerebrospinal fluid can predict which normal-pressure hydrocephalus patients will respond well to shunt surgery. Normal-pressure hydrocephalus is a condition causing gait, cognitive, and bladder problems that can sometimes be treated by draining excess cerebrospinal fluid via a shunt. The researchers likely correlate biomarker levels with clinical outcomes after shunt placement to see if this marker could help select patients for surgery.
papers.why: This paper is only tangentially related to the profile, as it focuses on a clinical CSF biomarker and hydrocephalus treatment outcomes rather than mitophagy, autophagy, spatial transcriptomics/metabolomics, or interneuron/perineuronal net biology in neurons.

papers.title: Wastewater-Based Surveillance of Human Papillomavirus Genotype Diversity
papers.summary: This study uses wastewater surveillance to monitor the genetic diversity of human papillomavirus (HPV) strains circulating in a human population. By sequencing viral DNA collected from sewage samples, researchers can track which HPV genotypes are present without needing individual patient testing. This approach offers a population-level snapshot of HPV strain prevalence and diversity over time and location.
